text:
Verses 54-58

(7:54) Indeed your Lord is Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then He settled on the Throne. He draws the night’s cover over the day, which pursues it swiftly, and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, [all of them] subservient

by His command. Look! All creation and command belong to Him. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of all nations.

(7:55) Supplicate your Lord, beseechingly and secretly. Indeed He does not like the transgressors.

(7:56) And do not cause corruption on the earth after its restoration, and supplicate Him with fear and hope: indeed Allah’s mercy is close to the virtuous.

(7:57) It is He who sends forth the winds as harbingers of His mercy. When they bear [rain-]laden clouds, We drive them toward a dead land and send down water on it, and with it We bring forth all kinds of crops. Thus shall We raise the dead; maybe you will take admonition.

(7:58) The good land—its vegetation comes out by the permission of its Lord, and as for that which is bad, it does not come out except sparsely. Thus do We paraphrase the signs variously for a people who give thanks.

Introduction

These verses are connected to the previous set of verses and build on them. The main theme of the previous verses was to explain the unpleasant consequences of associating partners with God and rejecting His signs, which would cause eternal damnation and everlasting wretchedness for the person. These verses provide an argument to justify that by explaining that the Lord of all beings is One, and He alone directs the affairs of all. Hence, it is incumbent on everyone to call Him and be grateful to Him. These verses prove God as the sole Lord of the worlds in two ways: (1) He is the One Who has created the heavens and the earth, and Who directs their affairs in the best way, through an ordered network [of causes and effects] which connects all beings in the universe. Hence, He alone is the Lord of all beings. (2) He is the One Who provides for the people by bringing out all kinds of fruits and crops. He creates these products through the most brilliant and elegant way, which is the rain. Thus He is the Lord of everyone, and they have no lord besides Him.

Commentary

(7:54) Indeed your Lord is Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then He settled on the Throne. He draws the night’s cover over the day, which pursues it swiftly, and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, [all of them] subservient by His command. Look! All creation and command belong to Him. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of all nations. We shall fully discuss the meaning of “heaven” and the six days of creation in our exposition of Sūrah Fuṣṣilat [verses 41:9-12], by God’s will. … then He settled (istawá) on the Throne (al-ʿarsh). He draws the night’s cover over the day, which pursues it swiftly, and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, [all of them] subservient by His command …:Istiwāʾ means “being firmly established, positioned and ensconced on something.” Sometimes it is used synonymously with tasāwī (equality). For instance, it is said that “Zayd and ʿAmr istawá,” meaning that they are equal [in a certain property]. Similarly the Qur’an says: They are not equal with Allah (9:19).

ʿArsh (throne) means “the seat where a king sits.” Sometimes it is used metaphorically, indicating the station of sovereignty, dominion and majesty. Al-Rāghib says in al-Mufradāt:

The original meaning of ʿarsh is “something that is roofed.” Its plural is ʿurūsh, as God says: it lay fallen on its roofs (ʿurūsh)

(2:259). Similarly, when one sets up trellises for vine, one would say ʿarashtu al-karm. When one makes something that resembles a roof for something, one says: ʿarrashtuhu… ʿArsh can also be compared to the hūdaj (howdah, litter) used to carry women, because the hūdaj has the shape of vine trellis. When one raises a sunshade above a well, one says: ʿarrashtu

al-biʾr. A ruler’s seat is called ʿarsh since it is an elevated position… What we humans know of God’s ʿarsh is only a name. It is not what ordinary people imagine it to be, because then God would be carried on His Throne, not the carrier of the Throne, while He says: Indeed Allah sustains the heavens and the earth lest they should fall apart, and if they were to fall apart there is none who can sustain them except Him (35:41).

Some have said that ʿarsh (Throne) is the highest sphere (falak al-aʿlá), while kursī (Pedestal) is the sphere of fixed stars (falak al-kawākib).1 They support this interpretation by a Prophetic narration: “The seven heavens and the seven earths compared to the kursī are like a mere ring thrown in a vast plain, and the kursī

1 This is based on the Ptolemaic system which was integrated into neo-Platonic cosmology, all of which later composed the foundation of Islamic philosophy. It was thought that the material world consists of nine concentric firmaments or spheres (called afiāk) which are superimposed on each other. The highest of these, the ninth firmament, is a starless sphere called falak al-aṭlas. The one right below it, the eighth firmament, was the sphere of fixed stars, called falak al-thawābit. (Trans.)

compared to the ʿarsh has the same relation.”

It has been a consistent custom in all times to seat the heads and rulers of the society in an exclusive fashion that distinguishes them from others. They were provided with special cushions and carpets, and later on with special couches and seats. This way, the word ʿarsh started to convey the meaning of kingdom. It conveys this meaning to a more exclusive and highlighted degree compared to kursī, which includes other kinds of seats and positions as well. Due to repeated usage, the concept of “kingdom” was designated by the word ʿarsh (throne), just as initially the royal seat was known by the concept of “kingdom.” Thus the word ʿarsh began to carry the meaning of kingdom and represent the position of dominion and authority; that is the meaning which it reduces to. It refers to the focal point where all affairs of the society are planned and governed.

To better understand this, imagine a collection of people who gather in a place to form a country together, based on natural, economic or political conditions. They found an independent society of their own and start

interacting with each other and exchanging their products. They determine each person’s share based on the weight of the person’s contribution

to the society. Now, if they want to maintain their unity, they have no alternative but to have a leader who would take charge of their social order. We

know beyond doubt, based on repeated observations, that when a group of people form a single unit and pursue common interests, they cannot maintain their unity and solidarity due to the various forces and intentions involved, unless there is a centralized authority which brings together all differences. There must be a single body that maintains their unity and gives life to the community through its proper direction. Otherwise, the group will immediately disintegrate and break apart.

This is why we see that in modern societies, every affair is classified as a specific category or branch, headed by a certain office or administrative body. There is an intermediate “seat” (kursī) which directs and takes charge of the different branches. Then these seats, being themselves of several categories, are headed by a higher authority or “seat” that supervises them. And thus the system escalates to a single position which holds the reign of all affairs. That is the ultimate “throne” (ʿarsh) and the person who is seated in that position.

It is interesting how this authority is so extended and comprehensive despite its unity: a single command which is issued from the top authority trickles down to the numerous lower offices, taking a different shape in every level according to that level. It appears at every stage in a way that is meaningful to the person in charge of executing that stage of the command. The top authority orders: “Direct the affairs!” whereby the financial body adopts it as a financial directive; the political body adopts it a

political directive; and the martial body adopts it as a military directive. It is determined and delimited at every stage all the way from the top to the bottom.

Going from bottom to top, the infinitely many minor and particular acts and laws which are executed in the nation are collected and centered at intermediate “seats” in several stages of aggregation, until all affairs reach the ultimate “throne” where everything is combined and united. On the one hand, the throne is one, because it is a single position directed by a single authority. On the other hand, in its oneness it includes all the detailed and differentiated levels of authority which lie below it at the lower levels. Going from top to bottom, this oneness constantly multiplies and differentiates until it reaches the specific commands which are

applicable at the individual level in the society.

The above illustration pertains to our conventional systems of government. This conventional system is necessarily extracted from a similar

order in the world of creation. If one reflects on the world of existence, one would realize that it is governed by a similar order of authority: particular events are caused by particular means and forces, which are themselves caused by more universal forces, until they all end up in God as their ultimate cause. The difference there is that God is not a distant cause at one end of the chain, but He is there with every event and present at every level of creation; He encompasses everything. This difference is because God’s mulk (kingdom, sovereignty, authority) is real, while mulk in the human domain is conventional.1

This means that the reign of every cause and effect in the world of creation—despite their enormous diversity, multitude and levels—is gathered and held in a single stage of authority which is called “the Throne”

(al-ʿarsh), as we shall elaborate on it shortly. The Throne is a locus of all

1 In other words, God’s authority over something is based on Him being the source of existence of that thing, while human authority is based on social contract. (Trans.)

existential and creational forms (ṣuwar kawniyyah)1 which are directed by God’s command according to His will; And with Him are the treasures of the unseen (6:59).

… then He settled on the Throne…: This is a metaphorical expression to God’s command of His kingdom and His direction of all affairs in the world of creation. It refers to His all-encompassing authority which extends to anything big or small. It is the source from which the order of every affair in the universe issues, through which every being is directed toward its goal and meets its needs. That is why in a similar verse in Sūrah Yūnus God says: then He settled on the Throne, directing the command

(10:3). The verse means that the Throne represents the divine direction of affairs in the universe.

… He draws (yughshī) the night’s cover over the day…: The verb yughshī is synonymous with yasturu (covers, conceals, veils). It means: “God covers the night with the day.”2

…which pursues it swiftly (ḥathīthan)…: The night chases the day in order to cover and conceal it. Ḥathīth is synonymous with sarīʿ (fast, quick, swif ). This expression suggests that darkness is the primary state of the earth, and the day is an accidental quality which comes on top of the night because of sunlight. The night is the dark cone which always shadows half of the earth that is not facing the sun. Based on the verse’s imagery, it is as if the night is always chasing and assaulting the day. … and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, [all of them] subservient by His command (bi-amrihi)…: The three words at the beginning

of the phrase here—the sun, the moon, and the stars—are in the accusative form,3 meaning that they are the objects of Allah, Who created. This means

1 “Form” (ṣurah) here does not mean a mental image that is conceived by the intellect. Rather, it is meant in its ontological sense, as an undifferentiated stage

of existence of something, where it is not yet attached to matter. (Trans.)

2 The verb yughshī is ditransitive, where its direct object is “that which is covered” and its indirect object is the cover. Either object may come first. Therefore the verse can also be translated as: “He covers the night with the day,” which is arguably more apparent. Both the verse and the author have used masculine pronouns for day and night, which makes it difficult to discern the intended order. The idea that night is the cover can be confirmed with the verse: And a sign for them is the night, which We strip of daylight (36:37). The author’s subsequent exposition seems to support this interpretation. (Trans.)

3 That is, they are manṣūb in terms of infiection: al-shamsa wa al-qamara wa that subservient by His command serves as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier, participial phrase), describing the condition in which the sun, the moon, and the stars are created. The meaning would be: “And He created the sun, the moon and the stars while they are subjugated by His command”—they follow the course that He wills for them, toward a goal that He has willed for them. The letter bāʾ in bi-amrihi (“by” in by His command) indicates sababiyyah (causality or instrumentality).1 Several reciters have recited the three words with rafʿ,2 which makes them the subject of a new sentence, whose predicate would be: are subservient by His command.

Given the theme of the verse, this entire phrase—He draws the night’s cover over the day…—serves as an interpretation and elaboration for: then He settled on the Throne. We see a similar pattern in all verses which talk about the Throne [and the idea of God settling on it], where there is some reference made, either directly or indirectly, to God’s direction of the affairs of creation.

The Meaning of Creation (Khalq) and Command (Amr)

… Look! All creation (al-khalq) and command (al-amr) belong to Him. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of all nations: The word khalq is originally synonymous with taqdīr (measurement, determination, design,

arrangement).3 It means “putting two things together in order to define al-nujūma. (Trans.)

1 That is: “The world is made subservient because of His command, through His command, or by means of His command.” (Trans.)

2 That is, they are recited as marfūʿ in terms of infiection: al-shamsu wa al-qamaru wa al-nujūmu. The meaning would be: “And the sun, the moon and the stars are all subservient to His command.” (Trans.)

3 The inherent ambiguity in the word taqdīr, and the complexity of the context, both make it impossible to come up with a single English equivalent for the term. “Measurement” is accurate literally, while “determination,” “design” and “arrangement” are more pertinent contextually. To put it more simply, khalq can be compared with sewing a garment, where the tailor measures, cuts and arranges the different parts of a dress according to an initial plan. This illustration should make tangible what the author means in the following lines. Taqdīr means “defining the limits of something,” which is a way of giving identity to something and bringing it to existence. Thus the relationship between taqdīr and khalq (creation): the meaning of creation (khalq) is definition (taqdīr). Therefore, “creation ex nihilo” does not mean “turning the measures and bounds of something new.” However, in the context of religion it means “to originate and give existence to something ex nihilo” (ibdāʿ, ījād). The word amr has two meanings: (1) As a noun it is synonymous with shaʾn (affair, status, case, issue, condition). Its plural form is

umūr. (2) As a verb it means “to order, to command.” When one charges someone to perform an act, one would say: amartuhu amran. It is quite possible that the original meaning of amr was its verbal meaning, then the nominal meaning was deduced from performing an order. A command (amr) tends to give more structure and order to the life and affairs

of the one who is commanded. That is why one’s status and condition (shaʾn) in life is called amr. Then the usage of the word was generalized to other beings. The amr (affair, matter) of anything is an optimal condition which puts the affairs of that thing into order and gives direction to

its various aspects, movements, actions and objectives. For instance, it is said, “The amr of a servant is up to his master”; “The amr of wealth is up to its owner”; and “The amr of a person is up to his Lord.” All these statements express who is in charge of directing and managing the life and

affairs of that person or thing.

The plural form of the first meaning of amr—the nominal sense, synonymous with shaʾn—is umūr, while the plural form of the second meaning—the verbal sense, which is the opposite of nahy (to prohibit, to forbid)—is awāmir. It may be objected that this difference shows that they are two different terms, and one cannot be reduced to another. However, this is not a valid objection, as there are many other terms that have a nothing into something” because that is arguably nonsensical and impossible. W hat is nihil prior to creation is the particular definition and determination of the object, not its existence. Hence, the proper meaning of khalq—or creation ex nihilo—is the delineation of the existence—which already is—into a particular definition and measure. This means that khalq is not the creation of “existence” (wujūd), but the creation of “quiddity” (māhiyyah). In simpler words, existence is not created, but definitions are created. Incidentally, this etymological analysis of khalq also has metaphysical significance based on the theory of emanation (ifāḍah). In the first stage, God’s effusion unfolds as formless and unbounded existence (called al-wujūd al-munbasiṭ), which can be compared to an extended fabric. Then it is determined and delimited into various forms and shapes, which gives rise to multiplicity. This determination of the universal into the particular is based on God’s eternal knowledge and plan, which includes all particulars in an undifferentiated form (called permanent archetypes, al-aʿyān al-thābitah). (Trans.)

similar case. Anyone who studies linguistics will come across several such alternatives [which are derived from the same original meaning].

Amr is like a medium which connects on one end to “the owner of command”—such as a master—and on the other end to “the one who is commanded”—such as a servant. Thus it is annexed and ascribed to both. Sometimes it is said, “the servant’s amr (matter, case, command)” as the Qur’an says: and his matter (amr) shall rest with Allah (2:275); and sometimes it is said, “the master’s amr (matter, case, command)” as the Qur’an says: Allah’s command (amr) is coming (16:1).

Everything has an aspect of amr (command, affair) which belongs to God, and this amr is defined and interpreted in the following verses: All His command, when He wills something, is to say to it “Be,” and it is. So glory be to Him in Whose hand is the kingdom of all things and to Whom you shall be brought back (36:82-83). “All things” in verse 36:83 includes any essence, quality, action or effect. Their amr, which is in the hands of God, is the word “be” (kun), which indicates ījād (existentiation, giving existence to an entity). God’s amr is the existence that He bestows upon all things, by which they come to existence. When He says to something, “be,” it becomes. This bestowed existence is connected to God on one end, and in this sense it is called “God’s amr (command),” which is the divine word, “be.” It is also connected to the being which is given existence, and thus it can be ascribed to the being as “its amr,” which again is the aspect of the being that traces back to God. This aspect is referred to as “and it is” (fa-yakūnu) in verse 36:82. The first aspect [which relates to God] can be called ījād (existentiation), and the second aspect [which relates to the recipient] can be called wujūd (existence, being).1 The Qur’an mentions various qualities and features for each of these two aspects of amr, which we shall discuss in its appropriate place, if God wills.2

1 Ījād and wujūd differ only in terms of perspective or relation, not in terms of

their reality and essence. The former is from the standpoint of the subject (the donor of existence), while the latter is from the standpoint of the object (the recipient of existence). Ījād means “giving existence”; wujūd means “finding existence.” (Trans.)

2 As mentioned above, the first sense of amr is synonymous with shaʾn (affair, status, case, issue, condition). The long string of words in brackets shows that amr translates differently based on context. It can be compared to the word “thing” which is general and vague enough to accommodate numerous possibilities. The first sense of amr, in light of its usage in the Qur’an, can best

To summarize: God’s amr (command) means giving existence (ījād)

instantaneously. His amr includes the existence which He gives to an entity in the first place, as well as the existence that He gives to its qualities and effects [which are subsequent to its essence]. God is in charge of not only the very essence of every being, but also how every being is structured and functions. Nothing is in possession of anything of itself.1 God’s khalq (creation) means giving existence (ījād) according to some measurement and composition. God’s khalq is sometimes in the form of adding different parts together, as when the different components are put together to

form the sperm, which then fertilizes the ovum, which then grows into a full human by feeding on nutrients from the body in proper conditions. And sometimes His khalq is not by piecing various parts together, as in the case of simple immaterial beings, where what is added to the being is not external components, but only the existential degree of the being, as well as the effects and functions of that being in its interaction with other existents. In other words, all beings are measured (muqaddar)2 and be translated as “matter,” in all its ambiguity. Nevertheless, the context always

makes it very clear what “matter” is meant in the verse. The word is often used in the definite form—like “the matter” (al-amr), “God’s matter” or “His matter” (amrihi, amruhu), or otherwise in the indefinite form—“a matter” or “some matter” (used with tanwīn)—but with sufficient contextual evidence that clarifies the import. In fact, the second sense of amr (command, order) can also be reduced to the first sense. The second sense is specifically applicable when the Qur’an attributes amr to God (amr Allāh). Given all of the usages of the term in the Qur’an, “God’s amr” means “God’s thing,” which, based on the context, can mean “God’s decree,” “God’s decision,” “God’s plan,” “God’s act” and so on. It is used equivocally in order to emphasize its ascription to God. Therefore, when the Qur’an says, “God’s amr,” “His amr” or “Our amr,” it is not the word amr which is of primary significance, but the fact that it is something from the divine. This is the most apparent and the least contrived interpretation of the word amr as used in the Qur’an. A review of all usages of the term in the Qur’an would prove this and remove any doubts about it. In the current verse of discussion (7:54), the contradistinction between khalq and amr shows that they signify the origin of the universe and its continuation. That is, amr here means the direction of affairs (tadbīr), which is represented by the Throne, as the author has pointed out. (Trans.)

1 That is, nothing is self-sufficient in the world of creation, whether in terms of its being or in terms of its doings. (Trans.)

2 Muqaddar here means “defined, delineated and determined.” (Trans.) created (makhlūq) by God, whether they are the most primary principles in existence [that is, simple immaterial beings] or compound [material] beings. God says: and He created everything and determined it in a precise measure (25:2); He who gave everything its creation and then guided it

(20:50); Allah is the Creator of all things (6:102, 13:16, 39:62, 40:62). These verses show that God’s khalq (creation) includes and applies to everything. In other words, khalq means giving existence to something according to some plan, measure and order, whether that thing can be differentiated into separate parts [as in the case of compound material beings] or not [as in the case of simple immaterial beings]. This is contrary to amr, which is existentiation without the aspect of taqdīr (measurement, design, arrangement). This subtle point is the source of two differences in the Qur’anic

usages of the words khalq and amr: (1) Khalq is sometimes gradual, as the Qur’an says: Who created the heavens and the earth in six days (7:54). However, amr is not gradual: And Our command is but a single [word], like the twinkling of an eye (54:50). (2) Khalq is sometimes attributed to other beings than God, as He says [addressing Prophet Jesus]: when you would create from clay the form of a bird, with My leave, and you would breathe into it (5:110); and He also says: So blessed is Allah, the best of creators

(23:14). However, amr, in this sense [of bringing something to existence] is never attributed to other beings, but is reserved exclusively for God. Amr is what functions between God and the thing which He wills to exist, like the spirit which is a means by which the body lives. Reflect on these verses: the sun, the moon, and the stars, [all of them] subservient by His command (bi-amrihi) (7:54); that the ships may sail by His command (bi-amrihi) (30:46); He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command (bi-amrihi) (16:2); and they act by His command (bi-amrihi) (21:27).

There are many other verses similar to those, where a certain phenomenon occurs “by His command” (bi-amrihi). The letter bāʾ (by) in these verses indicate either causality (sababiyyah) or company (muṣāḥabah).1 In short, khalq (creation) and amr (command) are two considerations

1 Based on sababiyyah, the meaning would be: “The event occurs because of God’s command, or through His command.” Based on muṣāḥabah, the meaning would be: “The event occurs with God’s command”; that is, “It occurs while it is in company of God’s command.” Both reduce to the same meaning effectively: “God’s command (amr) is what brings the event to existence.” (Trans.)

of the same essential meaning [of existentiation]. Khalq is a stage of creation which is subsequent to some taqdīr (measurement, determination,

design, arrangement). Therefore, it best applies to the creation of the very essence of the beings, because the process of giving existence to an essence involves the determination of its features and effects. Amr, on the other hand, best applies to the creation and management of the features and effects of the beings, and the general system of causes and effects through which they interact with one another, all of which is subsequent to the creation of their essences. This distinction is applicable when both terms are used together. Otherwise, if they are used independently, each term may be used for all stages of existence, whether it involves measurement (taqdīr) or not. The reader should reflect on this.

… All creation and command belong to Him…: Since the verse here talks about two things—creation (khalq) and command (amr), separated by the conjunction “and”—it suggests that the two are distinct from one another. As we explained above, khalq refers to giving existence to the very essence of the beings, while amr refers to giving existence to the effects of the beings and the order of their interactions. The two stages of God’s creation and command can be mapped onto two statements at the beginning of the verse: (1) Indeed your Lord is Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth in six days (7:54). This refers to the creation of the essence of the beings [which is gradual and based on a plan]. (2) Then He settled on the Throne. He draws the night’s cover over the day… (7:54). This refers to the arrangement and ordainment of a perfect system which puts the different aspects and affairs of the beings into an ordered chain. Therefore, the two stages of existentiation can also be inferred from the first part of the verse.1

Objection: Using the conjunction “and” does not necessarily imply a distinction between the two sides of conjunction. Otherwise, we should

1 In the original text of al-Mīzān, the author’s quote here is a mix of verses 7:54

and 10:3, which seems to be a mistake. Verse 10:3 provides a more explicit expression of the two stages of creation and command: Indeed your Lord is Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and then settled on the Throne, directing the command. (Trans.)

conclude that Gabriel is not one of the angels based on the verse: Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels and His messengers, and Gabriel (2:98). Response: What is meant is that there must be some distinction in one way or another, which could be a matter of consideration and perspective. Otherwise, it is wrong to use a conjunction between something and

itself [where the two sides of conjunction are identical, without any sense of otherness whatsoever], such as: “Zayd and Zayd came” or “I saw ʿAmr and ʿAmr.” In the case of Gabriel, even though he is one of the angels, he differs from them in terms of his lofty position, power, and nearness to the Lord of the Throne [81:20].

… Blessed is (tabāraka, from barakah) Allah, the Lord of all nations: That is, He is possessor of abundant good (barakah) which He descends upon those whom He sustains, which includes everyone in all worlds. That is because He is their rabb (lord, sustainer, nourisher, director). Discussion on the Meaning of God’s Throne Muslim scholars have a wide range of views concerning God’s Throne (ʿarsh), the meaning of then He settled on the Throne (7:54), and other similar verses. Most earlier scholars1 have held that verses like these are among the mutashābih (ambiguous) verses of the Qur’an, meaning that we should keep silent about their interpretation and defer knowledge of them to God. They consider it to be unlawful innovation (bidʿah) in religion if one investigates about the deeper realities of religion and tries to discover the facts that lie beyond the apparent text of the Qur’an and the sunnah. This view, however, is contrary to the rule of reason; nor is it approved of by the Qur’an and the sunnah. The verses of the Qur’an encourage the readers in the most emphatic ways to exert themselves in order to complete their knowledge about God and His āyāt (signs, verses, communications, revelations) through remembrance, contemplation and reflection.

The Qur’an constantly leads the audience toward further contemplation by presenting them with rational arguments. The sunnah (tradition) of the Prophet also confirms this through a wide range of narrations which

1 There is no clear dividing line to define “earlier” versus “later” scholars. It is a

relative classification which depends on the author who uses it. In case of the ʿAllāmah’s exegetical discussions, we can approximately consider anyone living after the 17th century CE (11th century AH) to be among the “later scholars,” and those living before that as the “earlier scholars.” (Trans.)

can be considered as mass-transmitted in terms of their overall meaning (mutawātir al-maʿná).

It does not make sense to endorse a premise but prohibit the conclusion which follows from that. These scholars forbid studying the underlying realities of the Qur’an and the sunnah—even a theological study which

admits the apparent doctrines of Islam according to the understanding of the public, and which tries to defend these doctrines by employing principles that are widely accepted among the believers. They categorically classify all such discussions as innovation in religion. We shall not

concern ourselves with this group. We leave them with their mentality. As with those who have discussed the topic, they have offered a variety of interpretations for God’s Throne (ʿarsh). Here we present and examine three views:

(1) What is meant is the apparent meaning of the term. ʿArsh is a physical object that looks like a couch with legs. It is placed on top of the seventh heaven, and God (Who is far exalted from what the wrongdoers say) firmly sits on it as a king firmly seat himself on his throne. Comment: This is the view of the mushabbihah (anthropomorphists)

among Muslims. However, it is against the Qur’an, the sunnah, and reason, all of which agree that the Lord of the universe is clear of being analogous to His creation, whether in terms of His essence, His attributes, or His actions. He is glorified and exalted above anthropomorphism. It should also be noted that most advocates of the above view have considered ʿarsh (Throne) and kursī (Pedestal) to be the same thing.

(2) ʿArsh is the ninth celestial sphere which envelopes the entire physical world. It is also called muḥaddid al-jihāt (determinant of physical

directions), and falak al-aṭlas, which is devoid of stars. The daily rotation of this sphere is what gives rise to time. Right under its inner layer is the kursī, which is the eighth sphere, where the fixed stars are located (called falak al-thawābit). Then underneath that are the seven firmaments which belong to the seven [visible] planets, where each higher sphere encompasses the sphere beneath it. The seven planets are in the descending order:

Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury and Moon.

Comment: This view is according to the Ptolemaic astronomy which offers a system for the movements of the heavenly bodies that are visible to our senses. Proponents of this view have matched what is mentioned in the Qur’an—such as the seven heavens, kursī and ʿarsh—with this system. As long as they find no contradiction with the apparent text of the Qur’an, they adopt the principles of Hellenic physics and astronomy. For the parts that are contrary to the apparent meaning of the Book, they reject them. Some examples of these contradictory principles of Greek teachings are: (i) Beyond the ninth sphere there is nothing, neither vacuum nor matter. (ii) The rotation of the firmaments is eternal. (iii) It is impossible to

tear and stitch the spheres (called kharq wa iltiyām). (iv) Every sphere is in direct contact with the other sphere [above or below it] without any distance or occupants between them. (v) The spheres are all of the same simple matter, and there is no hole or door in them.

These are contrary to the apparent text of the Qur’an and hadith, which say: (i) Beyond the Throne there are veils and curtains. (ii) The Throne has supporting poles and bearers [69:17]. (iii) God shall roll up the sky, like the rolling of the scrolls for writings [21:104]. (iv) There are angels

which reside in the heavens. Even the narrowest strip there is filled with an angel that is either bowing or prostrating [to God].1 They penetrate the heavens, descend from it, and ascend to it. (v) Heavens have gates [7:40]. (vi) Paradise is in the heavens, at sidrat al-muntahá (the Lote Tree of the Ultimate Boundary) [53:14], where the actions of people are taken at the end.

There are more points which apparently contradict the ancient theories of physics and metaphysics. Thus Muslim scholars who have held that the heavens, kursī and ʿarsh correspond to the nine spheres have rejected the above-mentioned principles because of their contradiction with the apparent text of the Qur’an and hadith. Yet, these fundamental contradictions

could not make them realize that what the Qur’an presents is a completely different system than what they have assumed. Later on, with the advent of new scientific discoveries based on solid empirical data, the previous theories were fiatly falsified, so these Muslim scholars had no choice but to abandon their comparison.

(3) ʿArsh does not represent an external object, but it is meant metaphorically. When the Qur’an says: then He settled on the Throne (7:54) or

the All-Merciful, settled on the Throne (20:5), it refers to God’s dominion and authority over the world of creation. It is rather common in Arabic to use istiwāʾ (settlement, establishment) on something for istīlāʾ (dominion,

authority, rule) over the thing. For example, there is a poem which says: Bishr was established (istawá) in Iraq, on his bed, While no sword was drawn, and no blood was shed.1 Alternatively, istiwāʾ (lit. sitting straight and firmly) on the throne indicates the commencement of directing the affairs. This metaphor is based on the image that when the kings want to give orders, govern their nation, and run the country, they ensconce themselves in their royal seats. Either way—whether sitting on the throne marks the start of directing the affairs, or having control over the universe—it is a change of state and a shifiiofiposition, while God is clear from any change or alteration. This is true about anything that indicates a sense of transformation and movement. No aspect of transition is applicable to God. In all such cases, what

undergoes change is the recipient. It is about some being which comes to existence, and this event is expressed through a verb [which indicates a temporal occurrence]. The verb is attributed to God since He is one end of it. It means that His mercy was applied to the thing which was originated. This is similar to other verbs used for God, as we say: “God created soon-so”; “He gave life to so-and-so”; “He took the life of so-and-so”; “He

provided sustenance for so-and-so.”

Comment: It is true that the wording used here—then He settled on the Throne (7:54)—is meant metaphorically, but the question is: Is there some reality indicated by this figure of speech? When we talk about authority, dominion, kingdom, rule, leadership, governance, mastership and other similar concepts, they all indicate conventional positions which we have set up to facilitate our interactions. They are rooted in social contracts that we have set up and assumed. They do not have an external reality except for their consequences which appear in the real world. We have discussed this point repeatedly in our discussion of conventional matters (iʿtibāriyyāt). While religious texts employ the same language that we use to describe our social conventions, they are not limited to mental constructions. There

are external realities which correspond to these terms when used by God. When concepts like kingdom, authority, dominion and supervision are used for God, they have the same meaning as when they are used in the human world, but their applications differ. In the case of God, they represent a real quality or relationship in the world of existence which befits the divine; but in the case of us, their applications are mental constructs and conventional positions which exist only conceptually. We

devise these concepts and positions in order to enforce their nominal implications. For instance, when we call someone a “head” (raʾīs), we do so in order to indicate that others—whom we call “those who are headed” (sing. marʾūs)—should follow his discretion and decision. It is not meant in a real sense; the person is not literally their head, and they are not bodies for that head. Similarly, when we call someone a “member” of a board or society, it does not mean that he is really a hand, a leg, a liver or a lung. What is meant is that the person is in charge of certain affairs in this group, in a way that is analogous to how each member of the body takes care of a certain affair.

God calls this “diversion and play” (lahw wa laʿib), where He says:The life of this world is nothing but diversion and play (29:64). Worldly objectives—such as beauty, wealth, children, priority, power and position—are

nothing but conceptual labels that are only to be found in the mind. If we engage ourselves with these things for any reason other than the pursuit of an eternal goal in the hereafter, then we are occupying ourselves with illusory matters and imaginary forms. Competing with others in order to acquire such positions is just like the contests of children where they try to win the game in which they are so immersed. The result is only a fanciful pleasure in one’s imagination, not extending beyond. It does not correspond to anything in the real world and has no real external effect. When God calls the life of this world “a play” and criticizes it for consisting of merely mental positions, how could He be the first of the “players” Himself?! He is far exalted from that.

Therefore, when God says: then He settled on the Throne (7:54), it is a simile that expresses God’s authority over His kingdom and His regulation of the affairs. At the same time, this expression represents a level of reality [called the Throne] where the rein of all affairs—despite all their variety and multiplicity—is held and controlled. The same can be inferred from other verses which mention the Throne and ascribe it to God, such as: and He is the Lord of the Great Throne (9:129); Those who bear the Throne, and those around it (40:7); and the Throne of your Lord will be borne that day by eight [angels] (69:17); the angels surrounding the Throne (39:75). As we can see, these verses apparently suggest that the Throne is a reality which exists in the external world of existence. That is why we say that the Throne in this verse—then He settled on the Throne (7:54)—has a corresponding instance in the outside world. It is not merely a figure of speech that is limited to the simile in the verse. In this sense, the case of Throne in this verse is different from many other similes and analogies mentioned in the Qur’an. For instance, in the Verse of Light [24:35], we do not claim that there is really a divine glass, a divine olive tree, or divine olive oil in the world of existence, because these are only mentioned as part of the analogy [without extending beyond]. However, in the case of the Throne, the Tablet, the Pen and the Book [of decree], the verses suggest that they represent external realities. The reader should reflect on this.

The Throne that is mentioned in verses like this—then He settled on the Throne (7:54)—refers to a position in the world of existence where all events and affairs in the world are controlled, much like the office of a king, which is a centralized position for managing the affairs of his entire territory. We discussed this in detail in our exposition of the verse. This is confirmed by the verse: then He settled on the Throne, directing the command. There is no intercessor, except by His leave (10:3). In this verse, directing the command is an interpretive addition which clarifies the meaning

of then He settled on the Throne. Thus the verse continues to say: There is no intercessor, except by His leave. The theme of this verse is to explain God’s role in the world of existence and creation (takwīn) as Lord and Director. Therefore, what is meant by intercession (shafāʿah) in the verse is also takwīnī (creational, causal, existential) intercession, which is the same as the system of causality that is found in the universe. The causes and forces at work in the world are means and instruments which intermediate between God [as the absolute and ultimate cause] and the events and

effects that occur in creation. For instance, God creates heat through the intermediation of fire. Likewise, He expands and melts objects through the intermediation of heat. The verse denies the causality of all things unless it is accompanied with God’s leave. This is the same as God’s unity as the Lord of the universe, which is stated at the beginning of the verse: Indeed your Lord is Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth (10:3). There is yet another point that is conveyed by the statement, There is no intercessor, except by His leave (10:3). It is saying that if a certain plan or arrangement is to be replaced by another plan, that replacement and the new plan will also occur with God’s leave. What happens in intercession is that the intercessor mediates between God as the ruler, and the

interceded side which is subject to God’s rule. Through intercession, God’s rule takes a new course and is applied through a different channel than before. For instance, the sun is an intercessor before God for the earth; its intercession serves the earth to receive light. Without the sun’s intercession, God’s rule—which works through the universal order of causes and

effects—dictates that the earth would remain in darkness. The sun’s intercession changes the initial divine decree of darkness to light. Similarly, if

there is a barrier that blocks the light—like a roof or a veil—it would be a second intercessor which asks God to alter His previous decree, such that the sunlight does not shine on the ground directly.

In other words, an intercessor (shafīʿ) is a cause that changes a previous rule. The verse [10:3] is saying that the working of any such cause

hinges on God’s idhn (leave, permission). What this means is that anything that occurs in the world is part of God’s universal plan, management and regulation of the world. There is no escape from His plan and

order. So when we seek to find some means or devise an alternative in order to overcome a certain decree of God, change the way it unfolds, and escape the divine system of causes at work in the universe—whether through external forces and powers, or through our mental deliberations and plans—our very efforts, means and alternatives are also part of God’s tadbīr (direction, management, regulation).

For instance, things of inferior quality “disobey” God’s will and “refuse” to accept higher forms and blessings due to their limited receptive capacity. However, their very refusal of a certain stage of growth means their acceptance of another stage of growth, and both are from God. Similarly, people oppose their Lord out of their ignorance and refuse to submit to His grandeur. However, their very defiance [to a certain divine rule] is an act of compliance [to another divine rule, and to the entire system].1 Thus when one plots anything, he is at the same time subject to

1 In other words, their “disobedience” is itself according to God’s system of causes and effects in the world. They decline a certain channel of God’s decree, but they adopt another channel, so they are still obedient to God’s universal God’s plot, as He says: Yet they do not plot except against their own souls, but they are not aware (6:123); yet they lead no one astray except themselves, but they are not aware (3:69); You cannot thwart [Allah] on the earth, and you do not have besides Allah any guardian or helper (42:31).

The opposing forces and causes in the world can be compared to the two plates of a scale: they move in opposite directions and one always weighs down against the other, but with all their opposition they serve the same purpose of helping the owner measure the weight of an object. Hence, the statement There is no intercessor, except by His leave (10:3) means that any opposing cause that intercedes and intermediates between God’s direction and its outcome is itself part of God’s direction in another way—through the divine leave. The reader should reflect on this.

The verse in Sūrah Yūnus [10:3] conveys two points: (1) God alone is the sole Director of all events in the universe. A similar verse that expresses the same point is: Then He settled on the Throne. You do not have besides Him any guardian or intercessor. Will you not then take admonition? (32:4). (2) The Throne is a position of directing the affairs of the entire universe and governing the world of creation. The same idea can also be clearly observed in these verses: [He is the] Lord of the Throne, the All-Glorious, Doer of what He desires (85:15-16). Another similar verse is: And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, celebrating the praise of their Lord, and judgment will be made between them with justice, and it will be said, “All praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of all nations!” (39:75). The connection here is that the angels are the intermediate beings which carry God’s

rule, execute His commands, and follow His direction. These roles and functions are expressed by describing them as surrounding the Throne. Another similar verse is: Those who bear the Throne, and those around it, celebrate the praise of their Lord and have faith in Him, and they plead for forgiveness for the faithful (40:7). In addition to mentioning the angels as being around the Throne, this verse says that there are some “bearers” of the Throne. This means that there must be some specific beings who sustain and support this lofty position, which is the source and locus of order. One can reject a specific rule of God only through another rule of His. All one can do is to change channels, but one cannot unsubscribe oneself from the entire plan altogether. One is always subject to God’s decree, and any means that one seeks works under the same order. It only changes forms, but the essence is the same. (Trans.)

all divine directions [that is, the divine Throne]. There is another verse which also talks about this idea [of bearers of the Throne]: and the Throne of your Lord will be borne that day by eight [angels] (69:17).

Now, we said that the Throne is a position where all affairs of the world are gathered and concentrated. It is the center through which God acts as the Lord of the universe. This means that it must comprise of the image, form or blueprint of all events in the world, at least in an undifferentiated mode. Everything must be present to God and known to

Him at that level. This idea is found in the verse: Then He settled on the Throne. He knows whatever enters the earth and whatever emerges from it and whatever descends from the sky and whatever ascends to it, and He is with you wherever you may be, and Allah sees best what you do (57:4). The subsequent elaboration here—He knows whatever…—is an interpretive addition which explains the meaning of God’s settlement on the Throne. This means that the Throne is not only a station of divine direction of all affairs, but also a station of divine knowledge, because it encompasses all things in its scope.

Given the nature and definition of the Throne, we can also understand why it exists eternally. It will be there when the creation returns to God for the final judgment, as the Qur’an says: And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne (39:75). It also exists during the lifespan of this visible

world, as mentioned in the verses which talk about the creation of the heavens and the earth [in six days]. It was also there in the stage prior to this creation, as mentioned in the verse: It is He Who created the heavens and the earth in six days—and His Throne was [then] upon the waters (11:7).

(7:55-56) Supplicate your Lord, beseechingly (taḍarruʿan) and secretly (khufyah). Indeed He does not like the transgressors. And do not cause corruption on the earth after its restoration, and supplicate Him with fear and hope: indeed Allah’s mercy is close to the virtuous.

Taḍarruʿ is “to express humiliation and servility.” It is derived from ḍarāʿah, which means “weakness and abasement.” Khufyah is “to be hidden and disguised.” It is quite possible that khufyah also refers to humiliation here, mentioned to emphasize taḍarruʿ. The connection is that when one entreats with humility, he almost becomes hidden and unnoticeable due to his abasement and degradation [of himself].

The last verse—Indeed your Lord is Allah, Who created… (7:54)—stated that God alone is the Lord of the worlds because He is the sole Creator of the world and the sole Director of its affairs. The current two verses serve as a conclusion to that. They order the audience to call God and be servants to Him. One must adopt a religion that is commensurate to God’s Lordship: He is the sole Lord of the world, both at the level of creation and direction of its affairs.

Supplicate your Lord, beseechingly and (wa) secretly…:That is, one should supplicate God with humbleness and without raising their voice, for that would be against the manners of servitude. Praying loudly would be a transgression of the limits of servitude: Indeed He does not like the transgressors. This is assuming that the letter wāw means the conjunction “and,” which shows that both conditions—beseechingly and secretly—must be met in supplications. Another possibility is that the letter wāw means the conjunction “or” (aw), which introduces an alternative. This means that one should supplicate God either beseechingly, which is normally aloud; or secretly, with a low voice. That is what servitude to God entails; and if one transgresses the limits of servitude: Indeed He does not like the transgressors.

Another possibility is: W hat is really meant by beseechingly and secretly is “loudly and quietly” (jahr wa sirr). The verse has replaced taḍarruʿ (beseeching, entreaty, humiliation) for jahr to clarify that being loud in supplication is against the manners of servitude unless the person does so out of taḍarruʿ.

And do not cause corruption on the earth after its restoration…: This command pertains to how people should deal with one another, whereas the last verse was about one’s relationship with God (as one’s Lord). The core message of religion with respect to human rights is that people should enhance their living conditions by eradicating injustice from amongst them, and dealing with each other in a way that helps them to have more taqwá (Godwariness, self-restraint), whereby they can achieve happiness in this world and the next.

… and supplicate Him with fear and hope…: Humans have always sought to serve a lord and worship a god based on these two drives. Fear and hope are two common ways which have led the people to arrive at religion throughout the history. Sometimes people would adopt and worship a god in order to be secure from its harm; and sometimes they would adopt and worship a god in order to reach some benefit through it. However, fear alone may lead one to despair and desolation, resulting in a total abandonment of worship; while hope alone may result in latitude and neglect with respect to the duties of servitude, again leading to

a total abandonment of worship. There have been many cases of both. That is why God commands both of these by saying, supplicate Him with fear and hope, so that each of the two qualities would check and balance the other quality, and prevent its unwanted consequences. This maps to a more universal principle which governs the world of creation based on the two factors of attraction and repulsion.

… indeed Allah’s mercy (raḥmah) is close (qarīb) to the virtuous (al-muḥsinīn, from iḥsān): Here God defines the above-mentioned qualities—of balance in worship and refraining from corruption on the land

after its restoration—as iḥsān (virtue, excellence, righteousness). The verse implies that those who respond to God’s call are the virtuous, which is glad tidings to them, because it means that God’s mercy is close to them. While the word raḥmah (mercy) is feminine, the verses uses it with a masculine adjective qarīb (close) instead of its feminine form qarībah. There are three possible explanations for this: (1) Raḥmah is used as a maṣdar (verbal noun, gerund) here, which makes it gender-neutral and thus capable of taking both masculine and feminine adjectives. (2) Some have said that raḥmah denotes iḥsān in this verse, which is masculine. (3) Qarīb is based on the faʿīl verbal patterns, which is sometimes equivalent to fāʿil (active participial noun, nominative case) and sometimes to mafʿūl (passive participial noun, accusative case). In the case of qarīb, some have said that it is the latter, which makes it gender-neutral and thus capable of taking both masculine and feminine adjectives. A similar usage is seen in the verse: What do you know—maybe the Hour is near (42:17).1

1 In verse 42:17, “Hour” (sāʿah) is a feminine noun, used with the masculine adjective “near” (qarīb). (Trans.)

(7:57) It is He who sends forth the winds as harbingers (bushran) of His mercy. When they bear (aqallat, from iqlāl) [rain-]laden clouds (saḥāban thiqālan), We drive them toward a dead land (li-balad mayyit) and send down water on it, and with it We bring forth all kinds of crops. Thus shall We raise the dead; maybe you will take admonition.

This verse is also about God’s Lordship, but specifically with respect to the return of creation to Him. What we read above was about God’s Lordship with respect to the origin of creation: Indeed your Lord is Allah…

(7:54).

The word bushr is originally bushur, which is the plural of bashīr (bearer of good news), much like nudhur which is the plural nadhīr (warner). “Mercy” in this verse means “rain.” The verse literally says: “He sends

forth the winds as bearers of good news before (bayna yaday) His mercy” [where the word “before” is omitted from the English translation]. W hat is meant by bayna yaday is “before, in front of, prior to.” The verse involves a metaphorical expression, where rain is compared to someone who is away from his family, then a herald comes before him and gives them the good news that their awaited traveler is forthcoming.

Iqlāl is synonymous with ḥaml (to bear, to carry). Saḥāb means ghamām (cloud). A single cloud is called saḥābah or ghamāmah, just as a single date is called tamrah. Clouds are thiqāl (lit. heavy, loaded) in the sense that they carry the weight of rainwater. Li-balad mayyit can be interpreted in two ways: (1) “For the sake of a dead land” or “destined for a dead

land,” where the letter lām means li-ajl. (2) “Toward a dead land,” where letter lām means ilá (to, toward). The rest of the verse should be clear. The verse’s argument is that the revival of the earth proves the possibility of the revival of the dead, because the two are of the same nature.

This is based on the metaphysical principle that similar events (amthāl) follow the same rules of possibility and impossibility. Those who die do not vanish into non-existence altogether, because their souls are preserved, although their bodies disintegrate. This is similar to the plants, where the parts of them which remain on the ground wither, but their roots maintain their vegetative life. The plant remains without any growth, but it reclaims it active life later on. Thus God brings the dead back to life. The universal revivification of the dead on the Day of Resurrection is like the particular revivification of the earth every year. There is more to add to this discussion, which we shall present in another place, if God wills.

(7:58) The good land—its vegetation comes out by the permission of its Lord, and as for that which is bad, it does not come out except sparsely (nakadan). Thus do We paraphrase the signs variously for a people who give thanks.

Nakad means qalīl (little, slight, scarce). Apart from the context, the verse itself resembles common proverbs which use the same imagery to state that good deeds and results issue from good sources, and evil deeds and results ensue from evil sources. In this sense, the verse can be compared to the sentence, Even as He brought you forth in the beginning, so will you return (7:29), which we discussed above. However, given the theme and context of the last verse, this verse would mean that the different shares of mercy that people receive is because of a difference on their

end; otherwise, God’s mercy is universal and unqualified.

Examining Narrations

What we observe in the books of narration is that the Companions of the Prophet never provided any real discussion of concepts like ʿarsh (Throne) and kursī (Pedestal). Nor did they address deeper Qur’anic realities, even topics that pertain to God’s oneness (tawḥīd). Instead, they were always content with the apparent meaning of religious teachings, and never explored beyond that. We see the same approach among

their Followers (tābiʿīn) and the early exegetes. The following accounts illustrate this approach.

(1) It is narrated from Sufyān b. ʿUyaynah: The interpretation of any description of God in the Qur’an is only to recite it and remain silent about it.

(2) Once someone asked Imam Mālik, “O Abā ʿAbd-Allah. He settled on the Throne (7:54): How did He settle?”

The narrator says: I had never seen Mālik enraged at anything as he was incensed by this statement. He started sweating, and the audience [that is, his students] dropped their heads [in silence and contemplation]. W hen he recovered from that state, he said, “The how is unintelligible; His settlement is not unknown; believing in it is obligatory; asking about it is innovation in the religion

(bidʿah); and I’m afraid that you are misguided.” Thus he ordered the man to be taken out.

Author’s comment: Apparently his answer is deduced from the following account. (3) Concerning the All-Merciful, settled on the Throne (20:5), it is narrated from Umm Salamah: The how is unintelligible; [the meaning of] sitting is not unknown; accepting it is īmān (belief, faith);

and denying it is kufr (disbelief, infidelity, heresy).1 Author’s comment: This was their [the Companions’ and the early scholars’] approach on this topics. We have not received anything from them except what is found in the words of Imam ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib and his descendants. Here we shall present some of what we find in their words. (iii) “It is by His glory and light that the hearts of the believers see…” This part of the hadith shows that the Throne is a station which outlines the system which governs the life and evolution of all beings. (v) “He is here and here, above and below…” Since God supports, sustains and bears the existence of all things, no place is empty of Him, while no place includes Him more than any other place either. This reduces to God’s active knowledge (al-ʿilm al-fiʿlī) of all things, which means that all things are present to Him without any veil. Author’s comment: We shall discuss a few points from this hadith one by one:

(i) “The Throne has many different qualities…” This supports what we said in the exposition of the verse, that God’s istiwāʾ (settlement, establishment, sitting) shows that God holds the rein of directing all affairs of

the universe. The same idea is confirmed at the end of the hadith, where the Imam says: “This is like when the scholars express their arguments in different words.”

(ii) “This is God’s knowledge about the modality and quality (kayfūfiyyah) of all things.” What is meant here is knowledge of the higher causes that give existence to things. There are two common usages for the word kayf (lit. how): (1) Sometimes it is used to inquire about the quality of something. This is classified as an accident (ʿaraḍī) in metaphysics. (2) Sometimes it is used to ask about the cause or reason for something, as one would ask, “How did this happen?” or “How did Zayd do this when he did not have the means to do it?”

(iii) “W hen used in conjunction, ʿarsh is distinct from kursī…” That is: ʿArsh and kursī are the same in the sense that they represent a station in the unseen realm, from which the beings manifest and descend into this world. However, when used together in one sentence, they convey different meanings because that station itself divides into two aspects. It consists of two gates which are not wholly distinct since they mirror one another. There is an outward gate which opens to our [visible] world, and there is an inward door which is behind it. The Imam explained this by saying: “Kursī is the outward gate of the unseen…”

(iv) “Kursī is the outward gate of the unseen: it is the starting point of all original things (al-bidaʿ), and all beings emanate from it.” What is meant by bidaʿ is beings without a previous model or example. “All beings emanate from it” because all beings have an original creation; they are not a replica of a previous version. An event would be badīʿ (original, wondrous) if its occurrence is unanticipated based on the conditions which gave rise to the events prior to it. In other words, an event comes

and replaces what was previously expected to occur. This means that origination (ibdāʾ) reduces to badāʾ (alteration, apparent change of the course of events), where God cancels the effect of one cause and replaces it with another.

Therefore, all events that occur in this world—which emanate from the working of opposing causes and varying forces—are original events. They are results of an alteration or a new course of the divine will (called badāʾ). Yet, above the opposing causes and varying wills which constantly conflict with one another, there is a single cause and will which governs them all. It is the effect of that cause and will which always occurs. That [governing cause and overriding will] is what cancels one cause with another, changes what a setting entails by introducing something new, and restricts the impact of every force with something else. Imagine a traveler who decides to move on a path toward a certain destination. He launches on his journey, but after moving for a while he may stop to rest a bit. His act of stopping opposes his act of moving, and the decision to stop cancels the decision to move. However, both of them are subject to a higher will which governs them and arranges when to give priority to which. Each of these two wills—that is, the will to move and the will to stop—has its own function, which is the opposite of the other. Yet, they are both compliant to the will above them. They agree with each other in executing what the higher cause dictates to them.1 Hence, we have two levels here: (1) the stage where the different causes become distinct from one another and start opposing each other; (2) the stage where all causes are united together in harmony. The former corresponds to the kursī, and the latter corresponds to the ʿarsh. Evidently

Kursī denotes the seat of a king’s officers and agents who execute his commands. Each of them decides about a certain aspect of the nation based on their discretion. That is why sometimes one office or “chair” (kursī) comes into conflict with another, in which case one must be given priority over the other.

(18) The Messenger of God said: If one does not praise God for any good deed that he does, but praises himself instead, he has disbelieved [or has been ungrateful] and has destroyed his deed. If

one thinks that God has given anything of the amr (command, matter, affairs) to the servants, he has disbelieved in what God has revealed to His prophets, because He says: Look! All creation and command belong to Him. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of all nations (7:54).2

Author’s comment: Complacency (ʿujb) [about one’s deeds] can be equated to kufr in two ways [based on the two definitions of kufr]: (1) It entails ungratefulness for God’s blessings [to do righteous deeds]. (2) It implies disbelieving that good deeds belong to God. In the second part of the hadith, the idea that “nothing of the amr is lefiito the servants” refers to their independent possession and command of things. It does not deny people’s subordinate control over their deeds and affairs as a result of God’s endowment and conferment.
